beats.say: A penny gets you a whole music library. And you never see the bill.
Choose eight CDs for a penny - the bait.
Pick a regular club plan - pay normal price per album.
Select the auto-ship option - you'll get the next pick unless you opt out.
Members had to buy a minimum number of albums at regular club prices. Sounds generous.
But it does a job: a negative-option trap.
The auto-ship clause forces a purchase once the deadline passes, turning the penny into a hidden charge.
Revenue hit $1.4 billion in 1996, proving the model worked at scale.
By 2014 revenue fell to $17 million, and the parent filed for bankruptcy in August 2015.
You see it everywhere: a bakery offers a free loaf for $0.99, then adds a mandatory pastry purchase.
A gym sells a $1 trial membership, then enrolls you in a monthly plan unless you cancel.
The forced-purchase option now looks like the smart choice because the free item disappears.
Watch the fine print for hidden obligations. Follow for more.
